questions.question:
Assertion (A): India is the world's largest producer of sugarcane.
Reasoning (R): Sugarcane is mainly grown in the tropical and sub-tropical regions of India, where the climate is favorable for its cultivation, and it is also a high-demand food crop.

options.a: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
options.b: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution: (d) (A) is false but (R) is true. Brazil is the world's largest producer of sugarcane; India is second. R is a correct statement. (Some school keys mark (a), treating India as largest; factually (d).)

questions.question:
Assertion: Composting is an effective method of managing biomedical waste.
Reasoning: Composting converts biomedical waste into nutrient-rich soil, which can be used for gardening and agriculture.

options.a: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution: (d) Both (A) and (R) are false. Biomedical waste is infectious/hazardous and is treated by incineration, autoclaving or deep burial, not composting; composting is for organic kitchen/garden waste.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: List four factors that affect the climate of India.
questions.solution: Any four: latitude (Tropic of Cancer divides India); altitude; distance from the sea (continentality); the Himalayas (relief) blocking cold winds and trapping monsoon; monsoon winds; jet streams; western disturbances / tropical cyclones.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Differentiate between: Retreating South-west and South-west monsoon seasons.
questions.solution: South-west monsoon (June-September): moist winds blow from the sea (south-west) to the land and give widespread heavy rainfall over most of India. Retreating monsoon (October-November): winds withdraw from the land towards the sea (from the north-east), the weather is mostly dry with 'October heat' over the north, and rain falls mainly on the Coromandel (Tamil Nadu) coast.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Study the climatic data of place 'P' and answer the following questions:
Month: J F M A Ma Jun Jul Aug S O N D
Temp (deg C): 10 11 23 35 39 42 40 33 30 25 13 11
Rainfall (cm): 2 1 0 5 15 62 71 81 59 12 10 3
(a) Calculate the annual rainfall.
(b) Suggest a name for this station and give appropriate reason/s for your choice of answer.
(c) Name the hottest month and wettest month respectively.
questions.solution: (a) Annual rainfall = 2+1+0+5+15+62+71+81+59+12+10+3 = 321 cm. (b) A station in the interior of north India, e.g. Dehradun (Himalayan foothills): the very large annual range of temperature (42 - 10 = 32 deg C) shows a continental interior location far from the sea, while very heavy rainfall concentrated in June-September (SW monsoon) with a little winter rain shows the foothill/northern location. (c) Hottest month: June (42 deg C); wettest month: August (81 cm).

marking_points.point: Interior northern station with reason (large range, monsoon rain)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II

Look at the picture and answer the questions that follow.
(a) Identify the season depicted in the picture. Name the month/s when it is experienced in India.
(b) How is this season economically significant to India?
(c) Write down the direction of the winds during this season. Do they bring rainfall? If yes, which part/s experiences rainfall?
questions.solution: (a) The cold-weather (winter) season / North-East monsoon, from December to February. (b) The light winter rain from western disturbances in north-west India is very beneficial for rabi crops such as wheat; the rain on the Tamil Nadu coast supports rice cultivation there. (c) Winds blow from the north-east (land to sea). Mostly dry, but after crossing the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and bring rain to the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu); north-west India also gets winter rain from western disturbances.

marking_points.point: NE direction; rain on Tamil Nadu coast

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.topic: Laterite for construction; alluvium ex situ
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason why:
(a) Laterite soil is useful for construction.
(b) Alluvial soil is ex situ in nature.
questions.solution: (a) Laterite is soft when wet but becomes very hard on exposure to air, so it can be cut into bricks used for building. (b) Alluvial soil is formed from sediments transported and deposited by rivers far from the parent rock from which it was derived, i.e. it is a transported soil.

marking_points.point: Hardens on exposure, used as bricks

(a) Which technique of farming did Madhesh see being practiced?
(b) How do you think this technique is helping the farmers?
questions.solution: (a) Terrace farming (step cultivation on hill slopes). (b) Steps cut on slopes check the speed of run-off and prevent soil erosion, conserve water for crops like rice, and make steep land cultivable.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Read the article on soil erosion and answer the questions that follow.
'India has lost over 1,500 sq km of land to 'catastrophic' soil erosion. New research finds Assam the worst affected, lost close to 300 square kilometres of topsoil. A new study has revealed a worrying trend for India's soil health. Nearly 30 per cent of the country's landmass is experiencing "minor" soil erosion, while a critical 3 per cent faces "catastrophic" topsoil loss, according to the research.' Source: https://www.downtoearth.org
(a) Define the term - soil erosion.
(b) Explain two reasons that might have led to such a situation.
questions.solution: (a) Soil erosion is the removal/wearing away of the fertile topsoil by agents such as running water, wind and human activities. (b) Heavy rainfall and floods of the Brahmaputra cause river-bank and sheet erosion in Assam; deforestation and shifting (jhum) cultivation on hill slopes remove vegetation cover; overgrazing and faulty farming practices loosen soil.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: List any one productive and accessory function of forests.
questions.solution: Productive: provide timber, fuelwood and raw materials (bamboo for paper, lac, resin, gum, medicinal plants). Accessory (protective/regulative): check soil erosion and floods, maintain the water table, regulate climate and provide habitat to wildlife.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Observe the picture carefully and answer the questions that follow.
(a) A tree found in the region labelled '2' is used to manufacture beauty products. Identify the tree and the natural vegetation it belongs to.
(b) Write down the climatic conditions of the natural vegetation labelled '3'.
(c) A unique adaptation of the forests found in region '1' is ______ because ______.
questions.solution: (a) Region 2 is western Rajasthan: Tropical desert (thorn) vegetation; the tree is Neem (used in cosmetics/soaps; henna also accepted). (b) Region 3 is Himalayan (mountain/montane) vegetation: temperature decreases with altitude, cool temperate to alpine climate, heavy rainfall on lower slopes and snowfall at higher altitudes. (c) Region 1 is the Sundarbans (littoral/mangrove/tidal forests): breathing roots (pneumatophores) grow upward because the soil is waterlogged and saline, lacking oxygen (also stilt roots for support in soft mud).
questions.figure_desc: Natural vegetation map of India with regions 1 (Sundarbans delta), 2 (western Rajasthan) and 3 (Jammu & Kashmir Himalaya) marked

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.topic: Drip irrigation vs well; Persian wheel
questions.question:
(a) Observe the pictures and answer the questions. [Picture A: drip irrigation system with pump, mainline, laterals and drippers; Picture B: a traditional well with a pulley and bucket.] Write one way in which technique 'A' is advantageous over 'B'.
(b) [Picture: a Persian wheel turned by a camel.] Identify the technique. Name any two places in the North where it is used for irrigation.
questions.solution: (a) Drip irrigation delivers water drop by drop directly to the plant roots, saving water (little evaporation/seepage loss) and labour, and can irrigate a large area evenly, unlike lifting water by bucket from a well. (b) Persian wheel (Rahat); used in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh.
questions.figure_desc: Diagrams of drip irrigation (A), a traditional well (B) and a camel-driven Persian wheel

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Mention one advantage and disadvantage each of Tubewell.
questions.solution: Advantage: can irrigate a large area at any time of the year, independent of rainfall. Disadvantage: over-use lowers the water table; costly to install and needs a regular supply of electricity.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.topic: Need for irrigation; tanks in AP; sprinklers
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason why:
(a) India relies on irrigation for agriculture.
(b) Tanks are a common irrigation technique in Andhra Pradesh.
(c) Sprinkler irrigation helps in effective usage of water.
questions.solution: (a) Monsoon rainfall is seasonal, uneven and uncertain, with a long dry season; HYV crops and multiple cropping need assured water. (b) The hard, rocky, undulating Deccan surface makes digging canals and wells difficult; rivers are seasonal and depressions can easily store rainwater by building embankments. (c) Water is sprayed like rain only where needed, reducing loss by seepage and run-off; it suits uneven land and sandy soils and saves 30-50 percent water.

marking_points.point: Hard rocky terrain, seasonal rivers, natural depressions

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Observe the picture closely and answer the questions that follow.
(a) Name the technique shown above. Identify the part labelled '1'.
(b) What is the part labelled '4'? How does storing water in it help?
(c) Mention one objective of using this technique.
questions.solution: (a) Rooftop rainwater harvesting; part 1 is the roof (catchment area) with gutter/pipe that collects the rainwater. (b) Part 4 is the recharge well/pit (filter pit) - water stored/led into it percolates down and recharges the groundwater, raising the water table. (c) To meet the rising demand for water / conserve rainwater and reduce run-off, urban flooding and dependence on groundwater pumping.

marking_points.point: Rooftop rainwater harvesting; part 1 roof catchment

questions.figure_desc: Diagram of a house with rooftop rainwater harvesting: roof (1), storage tank (2), filter (3), recharge pit/well (4)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason why:
(a) India is in a better position in terms of solar energy.
(b) Biogas is a sustainable energy source.
(c) Ethyl mercaptan is added to LPG.
questions.solution: (a) India lies in the tropics and gets bright sunshine for about 300 days a year with high solar insolation. (b) It is produced from renewable cattle dung and organic waste, which is continuously available; it is non-polluting and the slurry is used as manure. (c) LPG is odourless; ethyl mercaptan gives it a strong smell so that leakages are easily detected and accidents prevented.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Read the statement and answer the questions that follow.
Agriculture is an important sector of Indian economy as it contributes about 17% to the total GDP and provides employment to over 60% of the population. Indian agriculture has registered impressive growth over last few decades. The rapid growth has helped Indian agriculture mark its presence at global level. India stands among top three in terms of production of various agricultural commodities like paddy, wheat, pulses, groundnut etc.. However, on the marketing front, Indian agriculture is still facing a lot of problems. Source: https://ccsniam.gov.in/
(a) Discuss one way how the growth of agriculture is benefitting the Indian economy.
(b) Explain any one problem that Indian farmers face that acts as a hindrance in the growth and supply of the different crops.
questions.solution: (a) It provides employment and income to the majority of people, ensures food security, supplies raw materials to agro-based industries and earns foreign exchange through exports. (b) Poor marketing facilities - lack of storage/cold chains and transport, and exploitation by middlemen, so farmers get low prices; also small fragmented holdings, dependence on monsoon, lack of credit.

(b) Tea is cultivated on hilly slopes.
questions.solution: (a) Jute fibre has a golden, silky shine and it is a cheap, versatile, valuable cash crop earning foreign exchange. (b) Tea needs heavy rainfall but water must not stagnate at its roots; hill slopes provide good drainage.

questions.solution: (a) Cotton; a kharif crop. (b) High temperature of 21-30 deg C with at least 210 frost-free days; moderate rainfall of 50-100 cm with bright sunshine during picking; well-drained black soil. (c) Gujarat and Maharashtra (also Telangana).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Answer the questions that follow based on the description given below.
The world is facing agrarian as well as nutritional challenges. Agricultural lands with irrigation facilities have been exploited to maximum, and hence we need to focus on dry lands to further increase grain production. Owing to low fertility, utilization of dry lands to produce sufficient quality grains is a big challenge. Millets as climate change compliant crops score highly over other grains like wheat and rice in terms of marginal growing conditions and high nutritional value. They can help to eradicate the plethora of nutritional deficiency diseases. Millets' cultivation can keep dry lands productive and ensure future food and nutritional security. Source: https://agricultureandfoodsecurity.biomedcentral.com/
(a) Give two examples of millets.
(b) Mention one reason why growing millets is an advantage to the farmer.
(c) Write down two geographical conditions that help in the growth the millet whose largest producer is Maharashtra.
questions.solution: (a) Jowar, bajra, ragi (any two). (b) They grow in dry areas with little rainfall and poor soils, need little irrigation/fertiliser and mature quickly - low cost and drought-resistant. (c) Jowar: temperature 27-32 deg C; rainfall 50-100 cm (cannot tolerate waterlogging); grows well on black/alluvial/sandy-loam soils.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Differentiate between an Agro-based industry and Mineral-based industry with an example.
questions.solution: Agro-based industries use raw materials obtained from agriculture, e.g. cotton textile, sugar, jute. Mineral-based industries use minerals as raw material, e.g. iron and steel, cement, aluminium.

questions.question:
Using the description as a reference, answer the questions given below.
The civil aviation industry in India has emerged as one of the fastest growing industries in the country during the last three years. It is the fastest mode of transport which has reduced distances and has led to drastic shrinking of the world. It is indispensable when speed and time are the main constraints. This mode of transport made a humble beginning in 1911 when air mail operation commenced over a little distance of 10 km between Allahabad and Naini. The British, French and Dutch introduced it in 1929-30.
(a) Identify the mode of transport discussed above.
(b) Discuss one advantage and disadvantage each of the identified mode of transport.
questions.solution: (a) Air transport (civil aviation). (b) Advantage: fastest mode, can reach remote and inaccessible areas (mountains, islands) and is vital in emergencies/disaster relief. Disadvantage: very expensive, cannot carry heavy/bulky goods economically, and depends on weather.

questions.topic: Roads, Ganga navigation, railways in NE
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason why:
(a) Road transport is the most preferred mode of transport.
(b) River Ganga is navigable throughout the year.
(c) Railways is not the common mode of transport in North-east India.
questions.solution: (a) Roads provide door-to-door service, are cheaper for short distances, can be built in hilly/remote areas and feed other modes of transport. (b) The Ganga is perennial (snow-fed from the Himalayas and monsoon-fed) and flows over a flat plain with gentle gradient and no rapids/waterfalls. (c) Rugged hilly terrain, dense forests, heavy rainfall, landslides and swift rivers make laying tracks difficult and costly; sparse population.

marking_points.point: Rugged terrain, heavy rain, high cost

questions.question: Imagine you have been appointed as the environment minister of your school. What possible and practical steps will you incorporate for the effective management of waste generated in the institution. Mention any two of them.
questions.solution: Any two: place separate colour-coded bins for wet (biodegradable) and dry waste to segregate at source; set up a compost/vermicompost pit for canteen and garden waste; ban single-use plastics and encourage reusable bottles/tiffins; paper recycling drives; awareness campaigns by an eco-club.

questions.question: List two reasons why there is a need for waste management.
questions.solution: Uncollected waste causes air, water and soil pollution and spreads diseases (breeding of flies, rats, mosquitoes); proper management recovers resources by recycling/composting and reduces load on landfills.

questions.question:
Below are the two pictures of disposing waste and its management. Note the pictures carefully and answer the questions that follow.
(a) Identify the techniques labelled '1' and '2'
(b) Mention two advantages that the waste management technique '2' has over technique '1'
questions.solution: (a) 1 - Landfill / open dumping of waste (truck unloading garbage); 2 - Composting (compost bin with layers of leaves, grass clippings, soil, hay, kitchen and garden debris, straw and branches). (b) Composting converts biodegradable waste into useful manure that improves soil fertility, whereas landfills waste land; composting does not pollute groundwater (leachate) or release foul smell and methane, and needs little space.
